# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Evolution, Challenges, and Future Horizons

The introduction of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) revolutionized the management of coronary artery disease. However, the progression from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents and subsequent drug-eluting stents (DES) was consistently hindered by long-term complications, such as in-stent restenosis and very late stent thrombosis. These limitations paved the way for the concept of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS). Designed to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery to prevent early recoil and restenosis, BVS gradually resorb over time, ideally restoring physiological vasomotion, facilitating positive remodeling, and preserving future options for surgical revascularization.

The paradigm of "leaving nothing behind" began with the non-drug-eluting Igaki-Tamai polymeric stent [1]. This was followed by the development of the first-in-man everolimus-eluting Absorb BVS (poly-L-lactic acid [PLLA] platform), which demonstrated initial safety and feasibility in the ABSORB Cohort A [2] and Cohort B [3,4] trials. Based on these encouraging early findings, BVS was hailed as the "fourth revolution" in interventional cardiology.

However, large-scale, randomized clinical trials tempering this enthusiasm soon emerged. The pivotal ABSORB III trial demonstrated non-inferiority of the Absorb BVS compared to metallic everolimus-eluting stents (EES) for target lesion failure (TLF) at one year, but noted a worrisome trend toward higher rates of device thrombosis and target vessel myocardial infarction [5]. At three years, the safety signals became more pronounced, showing a clear increase in scaffold thrombosis [6]. The investigator-initiated AIDA trial corroborated these findings in a real-world setting, showing a significantly elevated risk of scaffold thrombosis, which prompted early safety warnings and commercial withdrawal of the first-generation Absorb device [7]. Subsequent systematic meta-analyses [8] and the ABSORB IV trial [9] further validated these concerns. Long-term, 5-year patient-level meta-analyses confirmed that the excess risk of TLF and scaffold thrombosis remained elevated up to the point of complete scaffold resorption [10]. This late catch-up phenomenon was also reflected in the 3-year outcomes of the ABSORB II trial [11].

Mechanistic studies quickly identified the primary drivers of these adverse clinical outcomes: thick struts (~150 μm compared to ~80 μm for modern DES) that disrupted laminar blood flow, slow resorption kinetics, and suboptimal implantation techniques. To mitigate these issues, the "PSP" (Pre-dilatation, Sizing, and Post-dilatation) implantation protocol was introduced. Clinical evidence highlighted that strict adherence to the PSP technique significantly minimized the risk of scaffold thrombosis [12,13]. Studies by Ortega-Paz et al. verified that optimized deployment using post-dilatation with non-compliant balloons improved clinical outcomes [14]. Registries like GHOST-EU [15] and clinical trials exploring complex settings, such as ST-elevation myocardial infarction (TROFI II [16] and PRAGUE-19 [17]), emphasized that procedural optimization and precise imaging-guided sizing were critical. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) and pathological evaluations identified malapposition, underexpansion, and scaffold fracture as the predominant triggers of very late scaffold thrombosis [18,19,20]. Regional trials like ABSORB China [21] and ABSORB Japan [22], alongside extensive pooled meta-analyses [23,24], ultimately concluded that first-generation PLLA scaffolds had a narrow therapeutic window.

Consequently, the focus of the interventional community shifted toward alternative materials and next-generation designs. Magnesium-based bioresorbable scaffolds emerged as a promising alternative due to faster resorption times (approximately 12 months) and superior radial strength. The sirolimus-eluting Magmaris scaffold demonstrated excellent safety and low thrombogenicity in the prospective BIOSOLVE-II trial at 6 months [25], 2 years [26], and 3 years [27]. Simultaneously, next-generation ultra-thin polymeric scaffolds, such as the polycarbonate-based Fantom scaffold [28] and the thin-strut MeRes100 PLLA scaffold [29], were engineered to reduce hemodynamic disruption while maintaining structural integrity.

Currently, the European Society of Cardiology guidelines recommend against the routine use of first-generation bioresorbable scaffolds in clinical practice outside of well-designed clinical registries (Class III recommendation) [30]. Nonetheless, the conceptual benefits of temporary vascular scaffolding remain compelling. Continued refinement of scaffold materials, ultra-thin strut profiles, and dedicated implantation protocols may yet realize the clinical potential of bioresorbable technology in the future.
